Note: Steve is coming in blind. One brief April conversation — that's it. Lead with curiosity. Questions before statements. Get him talking first, then reflect it back.

Opening

Warm, grounded. Reference Björn. 60 seconds max.
"Björn introduced us back in April — that conversation opened up something I've been thinking about since. You mentioned you'd just taken on a new portfolio with significant housing responsibilities. I wanted to come back, hear how it's going, and share what we've been building — because I think it maps directly to what you're dealing with."

Discovery — Get Him Talking First

Don't pitch yet. Listen. Let silences breathe.

Open

"You've had a couple months in this role now — how has the housing portfolio been going?"Full stop. Let him answer completely.

Go Deeper

"How much of your time is it taking up? And what's the board's appetite for changing the status quo?"The board question is the real one. Let him answer both.
"What's the biggest barrier you see to getting something done on this?"Understand what you're working against before you show the solution.

The Problem — Reflect It Back

Confirm you've heard him. Then add the external frame.
"So if I'm hearing you right — the core issues are [his words]. Does that feel like a fair picture?"
The frame: "The way I'd put it: Northern Health is an institutional organization trying to solve a regional problem with residential tools. And the problem is bigger than just housing — it's attraction and retention, burnout, isolation, turnover, hospital closures, community breakdown, childcare. It's everything that comes with trying to get people to come to and stay in these regions."

The Solution — Bring Him Along

Not a presentation. Build the picture together. Check in after each beat.
"I'd love to walk you through what we've been building — not as a pitch, but as a conversation. Stop me if something doesn't land."
Plain English: "We're building a Healthcare Housing Hub — purpose-built, hospital-adjacent, starting in Dawson Creek. Right beside the new $589M hospital: furnished accommodations for rotating staff and locums, childcare, clinic space for physicians, meals, property management — one roof, one operator, one invoice. Northern Health signs a master lease. You get the beds. We run everything. No landlord calls. No maintenance. No admin."
Proof: "We've been doing this at smaller scale since 2022 — we have units in Terrace housing NH staff right now. The DC hub is the next chapter."

Check-In & Next Steps

After the solution — check alignment. Don't rush to close.

Reality Check

"What do you think? Does this map to what Northern Health actually needs?"
"How would the board react to something like this?"Board made it a strategic priority Oct 2025. Let him confirm that.

The Close

"I have thoughts on next steps — but I'm more interested in whether they line up with where Northern Health is. What would a next step look like from your side?"
"What would stop this from moving forward?"
Appendix A

The Facility — Dawson Creek Healthcare Housing Hub

What We're Building

A partner operator in full-service healthcare housing infrastructure. Grassroots — supporting the health and well-being of staff, while delivering regional healthcare infrastructure to hubs, facilities, and small clinics across the north.

Not just housing — community, healthy living, clinic leases, daycare, and programming that supports the whole community. Part real estate management. Part developer. Part project scope and delivery partner.

A sole focus on the health and well-being of those who serve health to others. Backed by the University of Waterloo research team and best-in-class community programming and daycare.

Appendix A — The Vision

Every healthcare worker in the Northern Health region — wherever they work — knows exactly what they're coming home to.

Same standard. Same facilities. Same community. Same support. Prince Rupert to Dawson Creek.

Across the region
Prince Rupert Hazelton Chetwynd Fort St. John Dawson Creek + every NH region
The Consistency Promise

At full regional scale, every healthcare worker knows — without a shadow of a doubt — that Northern Health, its facilities, and its community support hold to the highest level of integrity. What they get in Prince Rupert is the same in Hazelton, in Chetwynd, in Fort St. John, in Dawson Creek.

That consistency becomes a message that travels. Friends, coworkers, people considering a move — they hear the same thing: wherever you work in the Northern Health region, we have the same standard there for you.

Weakness Becomes Strength

A broad region with many rural and remote locations has always been Northern Health's greatest challenge. At regional scale, it becomes the advantage.

Local communities — each one thriving on healthy living, high-quality service, and strong programming — become nodes of strength rather than points of strain. The infrastructure that once scattered effort now anchors it, community by community, across the entire north.

Healthy Living Builds Stronger Communities.
The outcomes are clear — and they compound across every region, every posting, every career.
Healthy Living Stronger Communities
